prompt.context: Our company is pitching to the President of the Salt Lake City International Airport next week, hoping to earn a big contract with the Airport moving forward. We know that the SLC Airport is the only commercial airport for more than 2.5M people in the greater Salt Lake City area, is the 21st busiest in the nation with 650 flights per day, and is owned entirely by the City of Salt Lake. The Airport President is a mayor-appointed individual who oversees all aspects of the airport's operation.
prompt.question: This is a highly structured case without a traditional framework. You will be asked a series of questions about the airport. First: off the top of your head, what are the most important things that the Airport President must think about?

clarifying_info.a: A passenger is measured by a person who passes through the airport, either to board or deplane an aircraft. People passing through on a layover switching planes count as one passenger.

clarifying_info.q: Do people dropping off friends at the airport count?
clarifying_info.a: No. Taxi drivers, Uber drivers, and people picking up friends are not passengers.

clarifying_info.q: Do pilots, flight attendants, and TSA workers count as passengers?
clarifying_info.a: No. We are only counting people who have a paid ticket to fly, not people at the airport for their job.

clarifying_info.q: Are we counting one-ways or roundtrips?
clarifying_info.a: We consider each visit to the airport. For example, a family of four traveling roundtrip from SLC to Los Angeles counts as 8 passengers (4 when they leave and 4 when they return).

clarifying_info.q: What are the decision criteria for choosing between the restaurant and the lounge?
clarifying_info.a: The decision should be based on the criteria you said was important for the President to consider in part one.

clarifying_info.q: What would be the revenues and costs of the restaurant and lounge?
clarifying_info.a: The restaurant would bring in a $15 check per passenger, and cost $6 per passenger. The lounge would cost $30 per passenger who enters, and cost $12 per passenger to provide.

clarifying_info.q: Does the airport already have either a sit-down restaurant or a lounge?
clarifying_info.a: No, the airport does not have either.

framework: Consider key stakeholder groups: Passengers, Airlines, Airport Vendors, Security, City Tourism, City Chamber of Commerce
Passenger experience: bad experience drives people to alternate modes or alternate destinations (e.g., drive, train, ski in Colorado instead)
Airlines: unhappy airlines fly to SLC less, hurting local economy, increasing fares, causing layoffs
Airport Vendors: affect passenger experience and represent local jobs; President acts as intermediary like a shopping mall manager
Structure answers using airport-specific terminology (e.g., 'passengers in the terminal', not 'customers buying widgets')

questions.prompt: How many passengers does the SLC Airport handle annually? (Approach 1: flights-based)
questions.guidance: Break down using known data: 650 flights/day, estimate average plane size, load factor. Show organized math and arrive at a reasonable estimate around 30-35M passengers per year.

math.setup: Use daily flights x seats per flight x load factor x days per year

questions.prompt: How many passengers does the SLC Airport handle annually? (Approach 2: population-based)
questions.guidance: Segment the 2.5M local population by travel frequency, then double to account for visiting passengers (planes are roughly half local, half visitors).

math.setup: Segment population aged 0-100 (uniform distribution = 25K per age year). Focus on age brackets with distinct travel behavior.
steps: Frequent business travelers (top 10% of workers, age 25-65 = 40 years x 25K): 40 x 25K x 2 trips/year x 45 weeks = 9M
Occasional business travelers (next 10%, same age band): 40 x 25K x 2 x 12 = 2.4M
Other adults 25-65 with families, 1 trip/year: 40 x 25K x 8 people x 2 x 1 = 1.6M

questions.prompt: The President is thinking about which of two projects to undertake: opening a sit-down restaurant in the terminal or opening a lounge. Construction costs are already accounted for through municipal bonds — ignore them. Which would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Structure answer using the stakeholder criteria from part one. Evaluate financial profitability first, then consider passenger and vendor perspectives. Business travelers dominate SLC traffic and prefer a lounge; existing food vendors would oppose a competing restaurant. Recommend the lounge.

math.setup: Compare profit per guest for each option
steps: Restaurant profit per visitor: $15 revenue - $6 cost = $9 profit per visitor
Lounge profit per guest: $30 revenue - $12 cost = $18 profit per guest
Lounge is 2x more profitable per user; restaurant would need more than 2x the traffic to win on total profit
math.answer: Lounge earns $18 profit per guest vs. $9 for restaurant; lounge is preferred

brainstorming.prompt: What are the most important things the Airport President must think about when running the airport?

categories.name: Passengers
ideas: Overall passenger experience in the terminal
Impact of poor experience: passengers switch to driving, trains, or choose alternate travel destinations

categories.name: Airlines
ideas: Airline satisfaction with gate operations and ground services
Landing fees and airport cost competitiveness
Route network — more routes attract more passengers
Risk of airlines reducing SLC service, raising fares, or causing layoffs

categories.name: Airport Vendors
ideas: Appropriate number and variety of vendors
Avoid vendor conflicts (e.g., existing food vendors vs. new restaurant)

categories.name: City & Stakeholders
ideas: City of Salt Lake as owner — budget and bond obligations
Chamber of Commerce and local business community

recommendation: Recommend the President pursue the lounge over the sit-down restaurant
The lounge generates $18 profit per guest versus $9 for the restaurant — twice the per-guest profitability
The SLC passenger base skews toward business travelers who would prefer a premium lounge offering
Existing food and counter vendors in the terminal would view a sit-down restaurant as a direct competitor, creating vendor relations friction
risks: If passenger volume using the lounge is substantially lower than restaurant foot traffic, total profit could favor the restaurant
Lounge pricing ($30 per entry) may deter leisure travelers and families, limiting addressable market
next_steps: Survey frequent flyers and business travelers on lounge vs. restaurant preference
Benchmark peer airports of similar size for lounge utilization rates
Model total profit under different usage-rate assumptions to stress-test the recommendation
